components.text: The inference must justify a timeless cause that can nevertheless act personally to initiate a universe.
The argument must exclude further natural cosmological reality as the relevant cause.
The inference must justify how a timeless, unchanging cause can be personal and initiate a temporal universe.
The argument must exclude further natural cosmological reality as the cause or context of the universe.
Design must discriminate evidentially between life-friendly and hostile or imperfect cosmic conditions.
The design explanation must avoid accommodation of every possible observation through revised divine aims.
Design must discriminate better than alternatives across both life-friendly and hostile features of the universe.
The design case must address possible life under different laws rather than assume only familiar life.
The argument must show that moral objectivity entails independence from all human ends rather than merely impartial assessment.
The argument must distinguish objective morality from absolute or transcendent morality without defining the conclusion into its premise.
The pro argument must justify why objectivity requires complete independence from human ends rather than merely defining it so.
It must exclude objective but nonabsolute human-relative moral standards.
Naturalism must justify what it positively affirms without confusing comparative confidence with proof.
The concession that reality beyond known nature cannot be proved must not be redescribed as proof that naturalism rests solely on faith.
Naturalism's burden posture must distinguish withholding supernatural belief from the categorical claim that only physical reality exists.
The design inference must establish a relevant possibility and probability space rather than assume known life exhausts viable outcomes.
A design hypothesis specifying life like us requires additional support for the alleged designer's aims.
The design inference must justify its probability space and its assumptions about what forms of life are possible.
A designer's alleged preference for life like us requires additional independent support.
Naturalistic restraint may rely on acknowledged ignorance rather than a categorical contrary cosmology.
The moral argument must exclude objective standards developed through collective human moral and legal practice.
A secular account must explain retention and improvement of rules by reference to welfare and liberation.
Naturalism's positive resources must include a non-supernatural account of normative practice.
The challenge is to explain how human practices can sustain objective moral standards without supernatural command.
Naturalism must offer a positive account rather than rely only on denial of supernatural grounding.
The claimed historical facts require adequate source independence and corroboration before supporting divine action.
The best-explanation claim must compare ordinary natural alternatives to the empty-tomb account.
The alleged facts require sufficiently independent historical corroboration before supporting a supernatural best explanation.
Ordinary natural explanations for the empty-tomb tradition must be compared with resurrection.
Naturalistic restraint can be supported by underdetermination rather than proof of one complete alternative.
The decisive issue is moral ontology—what makes values objective—not merely how humans learn and practice moral rules.
Human-relative or evolutionary origins must supply an objective standard rather than only explain widespread moral belief.
Collective agreement and welfare practices must be distinguished from the existence of binding objective values.
The reply must distinguish the ontology of objective value from human knowledge or acquisition of moral beliefs.
It must explain why evolutionary and collective processes do not themselves supply an objective ontological standard.
It must supply a positive supernatural grounding bridge rather than rely on epistemic gaps.
Historical reliability should be assessed by source criteria rather than a mandatory rule requiring evidence outside the New Testament.
The proposed criteria must actually establish the relevant empty-tomb, appearance, and belief claims.
Historical reliability should be assessed through source-critical criteria, not a categorical requirement of external corroboration.
The reply must address the independence and reliability of the specific resurrection traditions.
No decisive component of the moral objection is addressed.
Live further-natural alternatives are challenged by philosophical and cosmological support for an absolute beginning.
The argument claims a deductive evidential bridge beyond natural reality rather than an unsupported frontier speculation.
The beginning plus causal premise is offered as the specific bridge whose absence con asserted.
The reply must establish an absolute cosmic beginning strongly enough to exclude further past natural reality.
It must answer the coherence objection to timeless personal agency.
It must show why a beginning warrants a transcendent cause rather than merely epistemic restraint.
It must supply a causal bridge beyond nature.
Alternative-life uncertainty must address conditions required for matter, chemistry, and complex self-replication.
The reply must still show why life-permitting structure favors design rather than merely requiring some explanation.
The reply must show that the relevant changes prevent any complex self-replicating life, not merely life like us.
It must show why design remains discriminating despite theological flexibility and a largely lifeless universe.
It must still justify the probability comparison and design inference after narrowing the life target.
Miracle testimony must uniquely support supernatural causation rather than remain compatible with natural explanation.
Historical criteria must overcome concerns about corroboration and symmetry with rival religious miracle reports.
The resurrection hypothesis must be compared evenhandedly with analogous claims from rival religions.
A supernatural best-explanation claim must address rival miracle testimony and natural explanations evenhandedly.
The reply must explain why the stated historical criteria do not sufficiently corroborate the specific miracle claim.
No decisive fine-tuning component is addressed.
A deductive argument is not defeated merely because it is not an inference to the best explanation.
A deductive bridge succeeds only if each premise is more plausible than its denial.
The resurrection argument's explicitly inductive form is not covered by calling the principal arguments deductive.
The opposing critique must assess whether the deductive arguments' premises are more plausible than their denials rather than demand only explanatory comparison.
A deductive argument can constitute a supernatural bridge if its premises are adequately warranted.
The resurrection argument's inductive and historical warrant is not repaired merely by describing other arguments as deductive.
Immediate religious experience must provide a reliable method for selecting truth among incompatible divine claimants.
General logical consistency does not itself establish which religious experience is veridical.
The experiential warrant claim must account for sincere reports supporting mutually incompatible gods.
Immediate religious experience must include a method for discriminating among incompatible claimed revelations.
No decisive component concerning deductive validity is addressed.
The diversity of religious claims bears generally on supernatural identification but does not directly assess the resurrection evidence.
